questions.question: How do you reverse a String in Java?
questions.title: Reverse a String
questions.direct_answer: Use StringBuilder's reverse() method, or manually iterate the string backwards and append characters.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic String manipulation and StringBuilder knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a char array without knowing the cleaner StringBuilder approach, or reversing in-place on a String (can't — immutable)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both the StringBuilder way and the manual way, and note when each is appropriate

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The cleanest one-liner is new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString() — that's what interviewers expect you to know first. If they ask for a manual implementation to test your logic, iterate from the last index down to zero and append each character to a new StringBuilder.

content: StringBuilder way: new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString() — clean, no loop needed
Manual loop: for (int i = str.length() - 1; i >= 0; i--) sb.append(str.charAt(i))
In-place with char array: str.toCharArray(), swap with two pointers, new String(chars)
You cannot reverse a String in place — Strings are immutable, you always build a new one

beats.content: Call out edge cases: empty string returns empty, single character returns itself. A common follow-up is palindrome check — just compare the reversed string with the original.

sections.hook: Reversing a String is a classic warm-up question. Know the one-liner, know the manual approach, and know why in-place doesn't work.

sections.title: How to Answer
Key Points
content: Cleanest: new StringBuilder(str).reverse().toString()
Manual: loop from length-1 to 0, append to StringBuilder
In-place: convert to char[], swap with two pointers
Can't reverse a String in place (immutable)
Edge cases: empty string, single char, null input

questions.question: How do you count the frequency of each character in a String?
questions.title: Character Frequency Count
questions.direct_answer: Use a HashMap<Character, Integer> or an int[26] array for lowercase letters — iterate the string and increment the count for each character.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using int[] only (fails for non-ASCII), or not knowing getOrDefault/merge for cleaner HashMap code
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both approaches and when to choose each, plus find first non-repeating character using the frequency map

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Two approaches — choose based on what characters the input can contain.

content: int[26] for lowercase-only input: use char - 'a' as the array index, O(1) space, very fast
HashMap<Character, Integer> for arbitrary characters including uppercase, digits, Unicode
Clean HashMap pattern: freq.put(c, freq.getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1)
Even cleaner: freq.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) — adds 1 if absent, sums if present
First non-repeating character follow-up: build the frequency map, then scan the original string and return the first character with count 1

sections.hook: Character frequency counting underlies a dozen interview problems. Know both the array approach and the HashMap approach, and when to pick each.

sections.title: How to Answer
Key Points
content: int[26] for lowercase-only — use char - 'a' as index
HashMap<Character,Integer> for arbitrary chars
getOrDefault(c, 0) + 1 pattern
merge(c, 1, Integer::sum) — cleaner version
First non-repeating: build freq map, re-scan for count==1

questions.question: How do you check if two Strings are anagrams?
questions.title: Anagram Check
questions.direct_answer: Sort both strings and compare, or count character frequencies in one string and decrement for the other — both should produce zeros.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to check length equality first (early exit), or not handling case sensitivity
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Present both solutions with time complexity and explain which is better

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: Two strings are anagrams if they use exactly the same characters with the same frequencies — just in a different order. Start with the length check: if lengths differ, return false immediately.

rows: Frequency array int[26]: increment for s1, decrement for s2, check all zeros

beats.content: The frequency array approach is better — O(n) time and O(1) space. Always clarify two things: is the comparison case-sensitive? Should spaces count? Normalize to lowercase and strip spaces based on the answer before running the algorithm.

sections.hook: Anagram check is a top-5 string question. Present both solutions, state the complexity, and show you think about edge cases.

sections.title: How to Answer
Key Points
content: Early exit: check lengths first
Sort approach: O(n log n), simple
Frequency array: O(n), more efficient
int[26]: increment for s1, decrement for s2, check all zeros
Clarify: case sensitive? spaces count?

questions.question: How do you find the first non-repeating character in a String?
questions.title: First Non-Repeating Character
questions.direct_answer: Two-pass approach: first count frequencies with a HashMap, then scan the original string and return the first character with count 1.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying complex one-pass logic — two passes is cleaner and still O(n)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention int[26] for O(1) space when only lowercase ASCII, and the queue-based stream approach

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: The clean solution is two passes — both O(n), combined still O(n). Don't try to solve it in one complicated pass. Two clean passes are easier to explain and just as efficient.

content: Pass 1: build a frequency map — iterate the string, count how many times each character appears
Pass 2: iterate the original string again, return the first character whose count is 1
For lowercase-only input: use int[26] instead of HashMap — O(1) space
For arbitrary characters: use HashMap<Character, Integer> with merge() or getOrDefault()

beats.content: The reason you scan the original string in pass 2 — not the map — is to preserve the original character order. A LinkedHashMap would also preserve insertion order if you need to iterate the map instead.

sections.hook: First non-repeating character appears constantly in interviews. Two clean passes beats one messy pass every time.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicate characters from a String preserving order?
questions.title: Remove Duplicate Characters
questions.direct_answer: Use a LinkedHashSet which maintains insertion order and rejects duplicates — add each character, then collect back to a String.

interviewer_intent.testing: Set usage for deduplication with ordering
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both LinkedHashSet approach and StringBuilder + contains() and explain trade-offs

sections.standard_example: Java 17 app processing user input and generating reports

beats.content: LinkedHashSet is the natural fit — it rejects duplicates automatically and maintains insertion order. Iterate the string, add each character, then build a new String from the set.

content: LinkedHashSet approach: O(n) time, O(n) space — clean and readable
Alternative: StringBuilder + contains() check before appending — O(n squared) but no Set import needed
HashSet loses the original character order — only use if order doesn't matter
Collect to String: iterate the LinkedHashSet and append each char to a StringBuilder

beats.content: The LinkedHashSet approach is the one to lead with. If the interviewer asks for no extra data structures, the StringBuilder + contains() approach works but runs slower.

sections.hook: Remove duplicates while keeping original order — LinkedHashSet does exactly that in one pass.

sections.title: Key Points
content: LinkedHashSet: maintains insertion order, rejects duplicates automatically
For loop: for(char c : str.toCharArray()) seen.add(c)
Then: StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(); for(char c : seen) sb.append(c)
Alternative: StringBuilder + contains() check — O(n²) but no extra class
HashSet loses original order — only use if order doesn't matter
